title: Radiators and Blue Hour
premise: Zephyrine Yarrow returns to their mother Marisol's shuttered house to catalog her belongings and her silences, discovering that the mother they resented for leaving was protecting them from something older: a life before them, a band, a betrayal. When a late-night radio program broadcasts a song Marisol wrote and never recorded, sung by a voice Zephyrine half-recognizes, they track the singer to a coastal town where the past has been patiently waiting. There, in the company of the band's surviving members and a teenage girl who knew Marisol as 'Auntie Sol,' Zephyrine must choose between the tidy grief of resentment and the messier inheritance of forgiveness. The book ends with Zephyrine recording the song at last, in Marisol's voice's absence and everyone else's presence, letting the stranger in the photographs finally become family.
about_author: Ada Eastwick is the pen name of a former radio archivist who spent a decade cataloging orphaned recordings and the people who made them. She writes from a house with too many radiators, all of which clank at blue hour.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Quiet
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, first-person POV, arrives at Marisol's house the week after the funeral and begins cataloging rooms the way one catalogs grievances. The radiators clank at dusk; the silence is architectural. They find a locked cedar trunk and a photograph of a woman who is not their mother, or is entirely their mother. Beat: grief as a form of avoidance, the almost-saying beginning.

chapters.title: What the Radio Keeps
chapters.summary: Still Zephyrine's POV. Insomniac, they leave the radio on and hear a song they know by heart though it has never been recorded — Marisol hummed it as a lullaby. The DJ credits it to 'the Blue Hour Sessions, unreleased, 1989.' Zephyrine calls the station; the DJ, Ruthie, remembers everything. Beat: the ground tilts; the mother becomes a stranger.

chapters.title: Cedar and Ash
chapters.summary: Zephyrine opens the trunk: reel-to-reel tapes, a setlist, letters addressed to 'Z' that were never sent. A letter reveals Marisol left a band, a partner, and a promise. POV shifts briefly to Marisol's 1989 journal entries interspersed. Beat: the first crack in resentment; anger at being lied to replaces anger at being left.

chapters.title: The Town That Kept Her Name
chapters.summary: Zephyrine drives to Pelican Narrows, following the return address on the letters. POV stays close-third on Zephyrine, now less certain of their own story. They meet Dev Okafor, the band's bassist, now a boat mechanic, who greets the name Yarrow like a bell rung. Beat: the stranger's version of Marisol begins to compete with Zephyrine's.

chapters.title: Auntie Sol
chapters.summary: Zephyrine meets Juniper, sixteen, who knew Marisol as the woman who taught her chords behind the fish cannery. Juniper's POV, bright and unsentimental, shows a Marisol generous and present — everything Zephyrine was denied. Beat: envy of a teenager; the price of survival made visible in someone else's gain.

chapters.title: The Third Voice
chapters.summary: Dev reveals the singer on the broadcast: Cass Ilves, Marisol's partner, who recorded the Blue Hour Sessions alone after Marisol walked out — and who has been dying slowly in the house on the point. Zephyrine learns Marisol left to protect a secret about Cass, or about herself, the accounts conflict. Beat: rising tension; every witness owns a different mother.

chapters.title: Reel to Reel
chapters.summary: Zephyrine plays the trunk tapes with Dev and Juniper and hears Marisol's voice young, laughing, mid-fight, mid-love. The last tape is a fight between Marisol and Cass about a debt, a fire, a name. Zephyrine's POV fractures between witness and child. Beat: the almost-saying becomes almost-understanding; the climax approaches.

chapters.title: The House on the Point
chapters.summary: Zephyrine confronts Cass, who is sharp, unrepentant, and dying. Cass tells the truth: Marisol took the fall for a fire Cass set — an insurance fire that nearly killed someone — and vanished to keep Zephyrine from inheriting a fugitive's name. Climax: Zephyrine must forgive the stranger in the photographs, and the stranger is both women. Beat: fury, then vertigo, then a terrible tenderness.

chapters.title: Blue Hour
chapters.summary: In the days after, Zephyrine, Dev, Juniper, and a frail Cass gather at dusk to play the Blue Hour Sessions' missing song together, Zephyrine singing the harmony Marisol always sang. The radiators of memory clank and settle. Beat: forgiveness not as absolution but as taking the whole inheritance, debts included.

chapters.title: Everything the House Kept Warm
chapters.summary: Zephyrine returns home, finishes the inventory, and records the song properly, sending a copy to Ruthie's program and one to Juniper. The final letter to 'Z' is finally answered, in Zephyrine's own hand. Beat: resolution — the silence cataloged, the family found, the price of survival paid forward instead of hoarded.
